title: On the Structure of Educational Assessments
publisher: Measurement: Interdisciplinary Research and Perspectives (Lawrence Erlbaum / Taylor & Francis)
key_findings: Frames assessment as an evidentiary argument: what we want to claim about a learner, what observable behaviour would support it, and what situations elicit that behaviour.

Specifies a conceptual assessment framework of linked models: student (proficiency) model, evidence model (evidence rules that turn work products into observables + a statistical/measurement model that updates the student model), and task model (features of situations that elicit evidence).
Treats scoring as probabilistic reasoning (e.g., Bayesian inference) rather than summing points, which allows uncertainty about proficiencies to be represented explicitly.
Vol. 1(1), pp. 3-62; published with commentaries and an authors' rejoinder (pp. 92-101).
athar_applications: Primary design blueprint for ATHAR assessment: every case action must map to a named observable that feeds a named skill in the student model.
Justifies storing skill estimates as probability distributions rather than point scores.
limitations: Conceptual/technical framework, not an efficacy study: ECD makes an assessment's argument explicit but does not by itself guarantee validity.
Building full ECD models is labour-intensive; game teams often report difficulty aligning game mechanics with evidence needs (see ATH-SRC-0604).

title: Implications of Evidence-Centered Design for Educational Testing
key_findings: Describes five ECD layers: domain analysis, domain modeling (narrative assessment arguments, design patterns, Toulmin-style diagrams), conceptual assessment framework (student/evidence/task models, rubrics, measurement models), assessment implementation (authoring tasks, finalizing scoring rules, calibration), and assessment delivery (presentation, scoring, reporting).
Argues design patterns let teams reuse an argument structure across many tasks, lowering cost and improving coherence.
Vol. 25(4), pp. 6-20; a draft version is available as PADI Technical Report 17 (SRI International, 2006).
athar_applications: ATHAR should keep a library of 'reasoning design patterns' (one per skill) that case writers instantiate, rather than designing evidence from scratch per case.
The five layers map onto ATHAR's pipeline: research library -> skill/argument specs -> scoring specs -> case authoring -> runtime engine + dashboards.
limitations: Written for large-scale testing; game contexts add constraints (narrative, flow, player freedom) that the paper does not address.

title: Stealth Assessment: Measuring and Supporting Learning in Video Games
publisher: The MIT Press (John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Reports on Digital Media and Learning)
key_findings: Proposes embedding ECD-based performance assessment invisibly in gameplay so evidence is gathered from what players do, without interrupting flow.
Illustrates the approach with Newton's Playground, targeting qualitative physics, creativity and conscientiousness/persistence.
Argues such assessment can capture complex competencies (systems thinking, creativity, problem solving) that multiple-choice tests capture poorly.
athar_applications: Model for ATHAR's 'assessment without quizzes': evidence comes from investigative actions (what was examined, in what order, what was revised).
Open-access book usable as a training text for ATHAR's assessment designers (non-commercial licence; do not reproduce in product).
limitations: Short programmatic report with an advocacy framing; validity evidence is limited to early studies.
'Stealth' raises transparency/consent questions with minors; ATHAR should disclose that play is used for learning analytics.

title: Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game
key_findings: Embedded a Bayesian-network stealth assessment of problem solving (four facets: analysing givens/constraints, planning a solution pathway, using tools/resources, monitoring progress) in 'Use Your Brainz', a modified Plants vs. Zombies 2.
47 seventh graders with complete data played about 3 hours over 3 days; in-game estimates correlated about r = 0.40 with Raven's Progressive Matrices and r = 0.41 with MicroDYN.

Authors flag a small sample, Bayes-net parameters tuned on the same sample (overfitting risk), and a contrived classroom setting; they call for longer multi-session play to improve reliability and validity.
athar_applications: Realistic benchmark: even a well-built stealth assessment shared only ~16% of variance with external measures; ATHAR should expect modest convergent validity and plan studies accordingly.
Supports multi-session evidence accumulation before reporting any skill estimate.
limitations: Small N, single game, correlational validity only; no transfer test; parameters not cross-validated.

title: Applying Evidence-Centered Design for the Development of Game-Based Assessments in Physics Playground
key_findings: Presents a 10-step procedure for building game-based assessments with ECD, applied to Physics Playground.
Names two core difficulties: aligning game mechanics with assessment needs, and disentangling several competencies that one task evokes simultaneously.

Competency model nodes for agents of motion (ramp, lever, pendulum, springboard); observables per level coded Gold/Silver/None; Bayesian networks with conditional probability tables parameterised via a generalized partial credit model, revised iteratively; a node with no direct observables was removed.
athar_applications: Template for ATHAR's engineering process: competency model -> observables per case scene -> conditional probability tables -> iterative recalibration with pilot data.
Lesson: drop or merge skills that no task observes directly; do not report skills the game cannot see.
limitations: Describes design process more than validity outcomes; physics content is more objectively scorable than open-ended reasoning.

title: A meta-analysis of the cognitive and motivational effects of serious games
key_findings: Serious games outperformed conventional instruction on learning (d = 0.29; 77 studies, N = 5,547) and retention (d = 0.36).
Games were not found to be more motivating than conventional instruction (motivation analysis: 31 studies; difference not significant per the authors' conclusion).
Larger learning gains when games were supplemented with other instruction, when multiple sessions were used, and when learners played in groups.
athar_applications: Do not market ATHAR as 'more motivating' by default; motivation must be measured.
Design for multiple sessions, team play options, and explicit debrief/instruction around cases.
limitations: Heterogeneous games and outcomes; many small studies; effect sizes for complex reasoning outcomes are not isolated.

title: Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
key_findings: K-16 studies 2000-2012: games vs non-game conditions produced a moderate learning advantage (effect ≈ 0.33, 95% CI 0.19-0.48, k = 57).
Value-added comparisons: enhanced game designs outperformed standard versions of the same game (≈ 0.34, k = 20) - design matters beyond the medium.
Effects varied with game mechanics, visual/narrative characteristics and research quality; authors call for better assessment and reporting. Vol. 86(1), pp. 79-122.
athar_applications: ATHAR should invest in value-added A/B studies of its own design features (e.g., hint style, debrief) rather than only 'ATHAR vs no ATHAR'.
Narrative richness is not automatically beneficial; test it.
limitations: Mostly short interventions and researcher-built outcome measures; few studies target higher-order reasoning transfer.

title: A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games
key_findings: 65 studies, 6,476 adult trainees: simulation-game groups scored higher than comparison groups on declarative knowledge (+11%), procedural knowledge (+14%) and retention (+9%) (figures from author's practitioner summary).
Games that delivered content passively were no more effective than comparison instruction; games worked best embedded in wider instruction with debriefing and when learners had unlimited access.
Entertainment value did not moderate learning outcomes.
athar_applications: Fun is not the learning mechanism: ATHAR's learning value must come from active reasoning tasks + debrief, not from narrative alone.
Unlimited replay of practice cases is a reasonable design default.
limitations: Adult workplace training sample; generalisation to teens is uncertain.
Percent differences reported in practitioner summary; consult full article for standardized effects.

title: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work: An Analysis of the Failure of Constructivist, Discovery, Problem-Based, Experiential, and Inquiry-Based Teaching
key_findings: Argues from human cognitive architecture (limited working memory, long-term memory schemas) that minimally guided instruction is less effective and efficient for novices than guided instruction.
Guidance matters less as learners gain prior knowledge, since they can supply internal guidance (expertise-reversal logic).
Groups discovery, problem-based, experiential and inquiry teaching together as 'minimal guidance'.
athar_applications: ATHAR's free investigation must be scaffolded for novices (worked-example cases, structured evidence boards, prompts) and fade as mastery rises.
limitations: Critics argue the paper mischaracterises PBL and inquiry as unguided (ATH-SRC-0609); position paper rather than meta-analysis.

title: Scaffolding and Achievement in Problem-Based and Inquiry Learning: A Response to Kirschner, Sweller, and Clark (2006)
key_findings: Argues PBL and inquiry learning are heavily scaffolded and should not be equated with unguided discovery.
Presents evidence that scaffolded PBL/inquiry can be effective and that scaffolding reduces cognitive load in complex domains.
Stresses goals beyond content knowledge: epistemic practices, collaboration, self-directed learning. Vol. 42(2), pp. 99-107.
athar_applications: Resolves ATHAR's design tension: inquiry-style cases are defensible only when strongly scaffolded; the debate is about the amount and form of guidance, not inquiry vs instruction.
limitations: Partly a rebuttal; the evidence cited is mixed in quality and context.

title: Meta-Analysis of Inquiry-Based Learning: Effects of Guidance
key_findings: 72 studies: guidance during inquiry improved learning activities (d = 0.66), performance success (d = 0.71) and learning outcomes (d = 0.50).
Type of guidance moderated performance success but not learning outcomes; effects on learning activities varied considerably.
Too few studies to draw firm conclusions about age differences. Vol. 86(3), pp. 681-718.
A secondary German clearinghouse summary reports larger effects on research-skill tests (d ≈ 0.78) than on content-knowledge tests (d ≈ 0.37).
athar_applications: Every ATHAR case needs built-in guidance types (process constraints, prompts, status overviews, scaffolds, explanations); guidance is a feature, not a 'help' button of last resort.
Measure whether a learner succeeded with or without guidance - guidance level is part of the evidence.
limitations: Mostly science-inquiry studies; transfer to narrative investigation games is an inference.

title: Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?
key_findings: Review of PBL goals - flexible knowledge, effective problem-solving, self-directed learning, collaboration, intrinsic motivation - and the evidence for each.
Much of the evidence base comes from medical education; evidence is stronger for some goals than others; facilitator role is central. Vol. 16(3), pp. 235-266.
athar_applications: ATHAR's 'case' format inherits PBL goals; facilitator role must be partly simulated by the in-game mentor and partly given to teachers in school mode.
limitations: Evidence largely from medical students/adults; teen generalisation is uncertain. Key findings summarised from reviewer knowledge; abstract not retrieved this session.

title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
key_findings: Updates cognitive load theory 20 years after its 1998 statement, relating instructional effects to working-memory limits and element interactivity.
Open access (CC BY 4.0); vol. 31(2), pp. 261-292.
athar_applications: Case difficulty in ATHAR should be engineered as element interactivity (number of clues that must be held and related simultaneously), not just 'more text'.
Mobile UI must offload memory (evidence board, notes) to avoid extraneous load.
limitations: CLT has been criticised for measuring load mainly through self-report scales; detailed claims summarised from reviewer knowledge, abstract not retrieved.

title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
publisher: Psychological Science in the Public Interest (SAGE/APS)
key_findings: Rated 10 techniques: high utility - practice testing, distributed practice; moderate - elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaved practice; low - summarization, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery for text, rereading.
Ratings based on generality across learners, materials, criterion tasks and learning conditions. Vol. 14(1), pp. 4-58.
athar_applications: Build retrieval (recalling principles from past cases), spacing (revisiting skills across a season), interleaving (mixed case types) and self-explanation ('why does this clue matter?') into gameplay.
limitations: Evidence mostly on memory for factual/conceptual material; benefits for complex reasoning skills are less established.

title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
key_findings: Restudying beat testing at 5 minutes, but prior testing produced substantially better retention after 2 days and 1 week.
Restudying inflated learners' confidence even though testing gave better delayed retention.
athar_applications: Short-term in-session performance is a poor proxy for learning; ATHAR's mastery model should weight delayed performance more than immediate.
Learners' self-ratings are unreliable; do not use them as mastery evidence.
limitations: Prose recall in lab settings with university students.

title: Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis
key_findings: Synthesised 839 assessments from 317 experiments in 184 articles on distributed practice.
Inter-study interval and retention interval interact: the optimal gap between practice episodes grows as the desired retention interval grows.
athar_applications: Season structure: revisit each reasoning skill at expanding intervals; decay parameters in the mastery model should lengthen as a skill is re-practised.
limitations: Verbal recall tasks; extrapolation to reasoning skills is an assumption.

title: Assessment and Classroom Learning
publisher: Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice (Routledge)
key_findings: Review of classroom formative assessment: innovations that strengthen frequent feedback on learning produce substantial learning gains.

Covers student self-assessment, teacher strategies and the formative elements of systems like mastery learning; gains larger when feedback is task-focused rather than ego-focused. Vol. 5(1), pp. 7-74.
athar_applications: ATHAR's assessment purpose is primarily formative: evidence must lead to an action (hint, debrief, next case), not just a score.
limitations: Bennett (2011) [ATH-SRC-0656] argues the headline effect-size claims drawn from this literature rest on untraceable, flawed or dated sources and that 'formative assessment' is ill-defined; classroom/teacher context, not games.

title: The Power of Feedback
key_findings: Proposes a feedback model: feedback should answer where am I going, how am I going, and where to next, at four levels (task, process, self-regulation, self).
Feedback impact can be positive or negative; type and manner of delivery matter; feedback about the self (praise) is least effective.
athar_applications: ATHAR feedback after each case: goal reminder + process-level comment on the reasoning path + one next step; avoid generic praise ('you're a genius detective').
limitations: Conceptual model; quantitative claims rely on Hattie's syntheses, whose effect sizes were revised downward (ATH-SRC-0618). The three-question/four-level details are summarised from reviewer knowledge; the fetched abstract confirms only a model of feedback properties and that effects can be positive or negative.

title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
key_findings: 435 studies, 994 effect sizes, >61,000 participants: average d ≈ 0.48 (after outlier exclusion), well below the d = 0.79 previously synthesised by Hattie.
High-information feedback was most effective (d ≈ 0.99); reinforcement/punishment weakest (d ≈ 0.24); 21% of motivational effects were negative, mostly from uninformative rewards/punishments.
Very high heterogeneity (I² ≈ 83-86%) and funnel asymmetry in journal articles - feedback is not a uniform treatment.
athar_applications: Points and badges carry little information; ATHAR feedback must explain the reasoning gap, not only reward.
Expect variable effects; A/B-test feedback formats.
limitations: Heterogeneity and possible publication bias; feedback-level (task/process/self) variable could not be coded.

title: Focus on Formative Feedback
key_findings: Formative feedback is information intended to modify thinking or behaviour to improve learning; it should be non-evaluative, supportive, timely and specific.
Forms include verification, correct answer, hints, worked examples; timing ranges from immediate to delayed; learner and task characteristics moderate effects; ends with design guidelines.
athar_applications: Use elaborated, non-judgemental feedback; consider delayed feedback for higher-achieving learners and immediate for novices (to be A/B-tested).
limitations: Narrative review; guidelines are synthesised judgements, not meta-analytic estimates.

title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
key_findings: Meta-analysis (607 effect sizes; 23,663 observations): feedback interventions improved performance on average (d = .41), but over one-third of them decreased performance, not explained by sampling error or feedback sign.
Feedback Intervention Theory: effectiveness falls as feedback draws attention up the hierarchy toward the self and away from the task. Vol. 119(2), pp. 254-284.
athar_applications: Design rule: feedback must point to the task/process, never to the learner's ability or rank.
limitations: Abstract read via OpenAlex (2026-10-27 gap-fill); mostly adult/work and lab tasks; moderators described by the authors as poorly understood.

title: Effectiveness of Mastery Learning Programs: A Meta-Analysis
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 108 controlled evaluations: mastery learning programmes had positive effects on examination performance in college, high school and upper elementary grades.

Effects appeared stronger for weaker students; effects varied with mastery procedures, designs and content; programmes may increase time on instructional tasks, and self-paced mastery programmes often reduced completion rates in college. Vol. 60(2), pp. 265-299.
athar_applications: Mastery gates in ATHAR should be soft gates with alternative paths, because self-paced mastery can reduce completion; weaker learners may benefit most, so gates should trigger support rather than block.
limitations: Average effect size not retrieved this session (abstract only); older studies; completion-rate cost is directly relevant to self-paced apps.

title: Knowledge tracing: Modeling the acquisition of procedural knowledge
key_findings: Introduces knowledge tracing in the ACT Programming Tutor: each skill is a binary latent state updated after each opportunity using four parameters - prior knowledge, learning (transition), guess, and slip.
Mastery is declared when the posterior probability of knowing a skill crosses a threshold (classically 0.95). Vol. 4(4), pp. 253-278.
athar_applications: The guess and slip parameters are the formal answer to 'correct guess vs correct inference'; ATHAR's mastery model can start from a BKT-style update per skill.
limitations: Assumes binary skills, no forgetting, and one skill per step; parameter identifiability problems are known; designed for well-defined procedural domains. Parameter description summarised from reviewer knowledge; bibliographic record verified via Crossref.

title: Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models, and beyond: an overview of learner modeling techniques
key_findings: Surveys learner-modelling families - Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models (e.g., additive factors, performance factors), Elo-type rating systems and newer approaches - and how to evaluate them. Vol. 27(3-5), pp. 313-350.
athar_applications: Supports starting ATHAR with simple, interpretable models (BKT or Elo-style) and comparing them on held-out data before adopting deep models.
limitations: Overview; does not resolve which model is best for open-ended reasoning tasks.

title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
key_findings: Compares six SRL models (Zimmerman; Boekaerts; Winne & Hadwin; Pintrich; Efklides; Hadwin, Järvelä & Miller) on phases, (meta)cognition, motivation, emotion and context.
Concludes SRL models form a coherent framework that can be taught to students; meta-analytic evidence suggests effects differ by developmental stage/educational level.
athar_applications: ATHAR case loop can mirror SRL phases: plan (hypotheses, what to examine) -> perform/monitor (evidence board, confidence) -> reflect (debrief).
limitations: Review of models; does not provide game-specific evidence.

title: Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being
key_findings: Proposes three basic psychological needs - competence, autonomy, relatedness - whose satisfaction supports intrinsic motivation, self-regulation and well-being, while thwarting them undermines both.
athar_applications: ATHAR motivation design: real investigative choice (autonomy), visible skill growth with calibrated challenge (competence), team/club play (relatedness).
limitations: Broad theory; specific design implications must be tested in-product.

title: The Motivational Pull of Video Games: A Self-Determination Theory Approach
key_findings: Applies SDT to video games: players' perceived autonomy and competence during play are associated with enjoyment and preference for future play; relatedness matters in multiplayer settings. Vol. 30(4), pp. 344-360.
athar_applications: Supports measuring need satisfaction (e.g., short in-game pulse items) as engagement KPIs instead of only time-on-app.
limitations: Abstract not retrieved this session; findings summarised from reviewer knowledge; mostly entertainment games and adult/young adult samples.

title: Validity of psychological assessment: Validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning
key_findings: Presents a unified view of validity as an evaluative judgement about score meaning and use, with content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external and consequential aspects.
Identifies two main threats: construct underrepresentation and construct-irrelevant variance.
athar_applications: Writing fluency, reading speed and dialect are construct-irrelevant variance for ATHAR's reasoning scores; the design must minimise their influence.
limitations: Conceptual; operationalising all six aspects is demanding. Content summarised from reviewer knowledge; only the bibliographic record was retrieved this session.

title: Validating the Interpretations and Uses of Test Scores
key_findings: Argument-based validation: state the claims behind score interpretations and uses as an explicit argument, then evaluate its coherence, completeness and the plausibility of its inferences and assumptions.
Interpretations and uses are validated, not the test itself; negative consequences can make a use unacceptable. Vol. 50(1), pp. 1-73.
athar_applications: ATHAR must write an interpretation/use argument per reported score (learner badge, teacher dashboard, school report) and validate each separately.
limitations: Framework, not a method for any one game; requires sustained evidence collection.

title: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014 edition)
authors: National Council on Measurement in Education
key_findings: Joint AERA/APA/NCME professional standards covering validity, reliability/precision and errors of measurement, and fairness in testing; now available open access (English and Spanish).
Organises validity evidence by test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences of testing.
athar_applications: Reference standard for ATHAR's validation plan; especially fairness (accessibility, subgroup comparisons) and reporting precision with every score.
limitations: US-centred professional standard; not legally binding in MENA; free access does not grant reuse rights.

title: Sampling Variability of Performance Assessments
key_findings: Using generalizability theory, task sampling was the major source of measurement error in performance assessments; large numbers of tasks were needed for reliable scores.
Different methods did not converge: students' scores depended on which task and method were sampled. Vol. 30(3), pp. 215-232.
athar_applications: One case cannot yield a stable skill estimate; ATHAR must aggregate evidence across many cases/scenes and report uncertainty.
limitations: Elementary science/maths performance tasks; exact task counts depend on context and must be estimated with ATHAR pilot data.

title: A Framework for Evaluation and Use of Automated Scoring
key_findings: Framework for evaluating automated scoring of constructed responses: fit to the assessment's purpose/construct, agreement with human scores, relations with independent measures, generalizability across tasks and forms, and impact on subgroups.
Gives guidelines for combining automated and human scoring in high-stakes use and for maintaining systems as technology changes. Vol. 31(1), pp. 2-13.
athar_applications: Direct checklist for evaluating ATHAR's LLM rubric scorer before any score is shown to learners or teachers.
limitations: Pre-LLM; does not address prompt sensitivity, model updates, or verbosity bias of generative models.

title: Comparison of Human and Machine Scoring of Essays: Differences by Gender, Ethnicity, and Country
key_findings: Using TOEFL and GRE data, e-rater and human scores were similar overall, but agreement at the aggregate level can hide differences for particular gender, ethnic or country subgroups; notable exceptions were found. Vol. 25(1), pp. 27-40.
athar_applications: Every ATHAR scorer evaluation must report agreement separately by dialect region, gender, age band and writing-length bands.
limitations: Specific subgroup results not retrieved this session; pre-LLM scoring engine.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
key_findings: Documents LLM-judge biases: position bias, verbosity bias (preference for longer answers), self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning when judging.
Strong LLM judges reached >80% agreement with human preferences, similar to human-human agreement, on chat-assistant comparisons.
athar_applications: Verbosity bias is a direct threat to ATHAR's goal of not rewarding fluent writing; scorer audits must include length-controlled tests.
limitations: Evaluates chatbot answers, not student reasoning; agreement with crowd preferences is not validity for an educational construct.

title: Large language models and automated essay scoring of English language learner writing: Insights into validity and reliability
key_findings: Four LLMs (PaLM 2, Claude 2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) scored 119 ESL placement essays twice on separate occasions; GPT-4 showed the best intrarater reliability and good validity.
Performance differed across models and fluctuated over time; agreement with human raters fell slightly between occasions.
athar_applications: Re-score a fixed anchor set after every model or prompt change; treat the scorer as a versioned instrument.
limitations: Small essay set, English only, older models; validity = agreement with human raters.

title: Exploring the potential of using an AI language model for automated essay scoring
key_findings: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) scored 12,100 TOEFL11 essays; scores showed a certain level of accuracy and reliability against benchmark levels.
Adding linguistic features improved accuracy - i.e., surface language features carry much of the scoring signal.
athar_applications: Warning sign for ATHAR: language-proficiency features predict essay scores; reasoning scores must be separated from language quality.
limitations: Scores language proficiency (the intended construct there), not reasoning; older model.

title: Comparing the quality of human and ChatGPT feedback of students' writing
key_findings: 200 secondary-student essays: feedback from trained humans and ChatGPT was scored on five quality criteria (criteria-based, clear directions, accuracy, prioritising essentials, supportive tone).
Humans gave higher-quality feedback on every criterion except criteria-based; authors judged the practical differences not substantial given ChatGPT's ease of use.
Feedback quality did not differ by students' language status for either source, but both differed by essay quality.
athar_applications: Relevant to ATHAR's LLM debrief feedback: compare against trained human feedback on defined quality criteria before deployment.
limitations: Abstract read (2026-10-27 gap-fill); English writing; ChatGPT version of the study period; feedback quality, not learning gains, was measured.

title: AI generates covertly racist decisions about people based on their dialect
key_findings: Language models showed covert negative stereotypes toward speakers of African American English (dialect prejudice) even while overt stereotypes were positive.

Models were more likely to assign such speakers lower-status jobs, guilty verdicts and harsher sentences; alignment methods like human-preference training could mask rather than remove the bias. Vol. 633, pp. 147-154.
athar_applications: Strong reason to test ATHAR's LLM scorer for dialect effects: identical reasoning written in Levantine, Gulf, Egyptian, Maghrebi Arabic and MSA must receive equivalent scores.
limitations: Studied English dialects; Arabic dialect effects are plausible but unmeasured - ATHAR must measure them itself.

title: How People Learn II: Learners, Contexts, and Cultures
authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
key_findings: Consensus report updating How People Learn (2000) with emphasis on how culture and context shape learning, types of learning, knowledge and reasoning, motivation, and implications for schooling and lifelong learning.
athar_applications: Supports culturally grounded Arabic cases and attention to learners' identities and contexts as part of the learning design, not decoration.
limitations: Broad synthesis; US-centric evidence; key content summarised from reviewer knowledge (abstract not retrieved).

title: FTC v. Lumos Labs, Inc. - 'Lumosity to Pay $2 Million to Settle FTC Deceptive Advertising Charges for Its Brain Training Program' (press release)
key_findings: 5 Jan 2016: Lumos Labs and two co-founders settled FTC charges; $2 million redress with a $50 million judgment suspended.

FTC alleged unsupported claims that training improves performance at school, work and sport, delays age-related decline, and reduces impairment from various conditions, and that the company claimed science proved these benefits.
Order requires 'competent and reliable scientific evidence' before such claims; also cited undisclosed incentivised testimonials.
athar_applications: ATHAR must not claim improved school grades, IQ, real-world critical thinking or job readiness without rigorous evidence; marketing claims are governed by the validation plan.
limitations: Settlement of allegations (no court finding of fact); US jurisdiction - analogous consumer-protection rules in MENA need legal review.

title: Do "Brain-Training" Programs Work?
publisher: Psychological Science in the Public Interest (SAGE/APS)
key_findings: Strongest evidence is for improvement on trained tasks; weaker for closely related tasks; little evidence for distantly related tasks or everyday cognitive performance.
Many studies had design/analysis flaws; none fully met best-practice standards (active controls, preregistration, adequate samples).
athar_applications: ATHAR should expect near transfer (similar cases) before far transfer and design studies with active control groups.
limitations: Focused on cognitive-training tasks, not narrative case-based learning.

title: Does Far Transfer Exist? Negative Evidence From Chess, Music, and Working Memory Training
key_findings: Meta-analyses of chess, music and working-memory training found small-to-moderate effects that shrank in better-designed studies (e.g., with active controls); authors conclude far transfer rarely occurs.
athar_applications: Treat 'ATHAR improves general critical thinking' as a hypothesis requiring active-control trials, not a claim.
limitations: Short review; domain-specific instruction in reasoning (e.g., Abrami et al.) shows more positive results than general cognitive training.

title: When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer
key_findings: Proposes a taxonomy describing transfer by content (what is transferred) and context (knowledge domain, physical, temporal, functional, social and modality distance between learning and transfer settings). Vol. 128(4), pp. 612-637.
athar_applications: Use the context dimensions to define ATHAR transfer tests: same skill in a new domain (science vs history case), new modality (text vs data table), new social setting (solo vs team), delayed in time.
limitations: Taxonomy; does not by itself estimate transfer effects. Dimension list summarised from reviewer knowledge.

title: Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis
key_findings: 341 effect sizes from (quasi-)experiments using standardized critical-thinking measures: weighted mean effect ≈ 0.30, with heterogeneity.
Dialogue, exposure to authentic/situated problems, and mentoring were associated with positive effects; effective strategies exist for generic and content-specific CT across levels.
athar_applications: ATHAR's evidence-based levers: authentic case problems + structured dialogue (team debate, suspect interviews with reflection) + mentor feedback.
limitations: Effects are modest; mostly classroom instruction, not games; measures vary.

title: Assessing Critical Thinking in Higher Education: Current State and Directions for Next-Generation Assessment
key_findings: Reviews how frameworks define critical thinking, existing CT assessments and their psychometric quality, and challenges; proposes an operational definition aligned with shared dimensions and considerations for next-generation CT assessment.
athar_applications: Use as cross-check for ATHAR's skill definitions (analysis/evaluation of evidence and arguments, inference) and for known measurement pitfalls.
limitations: Higher-education focus; ATHAR's 13-15 band needs age-adapted definitions.

title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
key_findings: 53 studies, 166 comparisons: problem solving followed by instruction (PS-I) beat instruction-first with a moderate effect (g ≈ 0.36), larger (≈0.37-0.58) with high fidelity to Productive Failure design.
Effects favoured instruction-first for younger learners (grades 2-5) and for domain-general skills; moderated by grade level and duration.
athar_applications: Supports 'try the case first, then structured debrief' for 16+ learners on conceptual targets; caution for domain-general reasoning skills and younger teens - A/B-test sequence by age band.
limitations: Mostly maths/science conceptual learning; the domain-general finding is directly relevant and cautionary for ATHAR.

title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
publisher: Psychological Science in the Public Interest (SAGE/APS)
key_findings: Found almost no studies with the design needed to test the meshing hypothesis; those with appropriate designs contradicted it; concluded evidence does not justify learning-styles assessment in practice.
athar_applications: ATHAR should not personalise by 'visual/verbal learner' profiles; adapt on demonstrated skill and prior knowledge instead.
limitations: Absence of evidence at the time; does not rule out other forms of personalisation.

title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
key_findings: Two meta-analyses over 164 studies: explicit instruction beat unassisted discovery (580 comparisons, d = -0.38, 95% CI -0.44 to -0.31), while enhanced/assisted discovery beat other instruction (360 comparisons, d = 0.30, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.36).
Authors conclude unassisted discovery does not benefit learners, whereas feedback, worked examples, scaffolding and elicited explanations do. Vol. 103(1), pp. 1-18.
athar_applications: Corroborates ATHAR's 'guided investigation' stance: free exploration must be enhanced with feedback, worked examples and explanation prompts.
limitations: Abstract read via ERIC (2026-10-27 gap-fill; the OpenAlex abstract is mis-linked to another study); heterogeneous outcomes and ages.

title: Metacognition and self-regulation (Teaching and Learning Toolkit strand)
key_findings: Toolkit estimate: about +8 months additional progress on average, very low cost, high evidence strength (355 studies); page notes the impact can be difficult to realise in practice.
Evidence rating lost a padlock because many studies were not independently evaluated; developer-led evaluations tend to report larger effects.

Strategies work better embedded in usual curriculum content than as separate 'thinking skills' lessons; tasks must be challenging but achievable; evidence on closing the disadvantage gap is limited. Strand last updated May 2025.
athar_applications: Embed planning-monitoring-evaluating prompts inside cases rather than separate 'thinking lessons'.
Teacher mode must explain the metacognitive model; do not quote '+8 months' as an ATHAR outcome.
limitations: Average across school interventions, not games; months-of-progress metric is a conversion of effect sizes and has been criticised (critique not verified this session).

title: Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning: Guidance Report (Second Edition)
key_findings: Second edition published 13 Nov 2025 with recommendations in seven areas; emphasises explicitly teaching strategies for planning, monitoring and evaluating learning, embedded in subject lessons.
athar_applications: Source for ATHAR's school-mode teacher guide and for the plan-monitor-reflect loop in each case.
limitations: Recommendations themselves not retrieved this session (only the overview page); all rights reserved.

title: PISA 2025 Assessment and Analytical Framework
key_findings: Published 28-29 May 2026; PISA 2025 assessed reading, maths and science (science focus) and, for the first time, Learning in the Digital World (LDW) as an innovative domain, plus an optional English-as-a-foreign-language assessment.
LDW is defined as the capacity to engage in an iterative, self-regulated process of knowledge building and problem solving using computational tools and practices.

Competency model has two components: computational problem-solving practices (conduct experiments, analyse data, build and debug computational artefacts) and self-regulated learning processes (monitor progress and adapt strategies, maintain motivation and task engagement, evaluate performance).
Test: two 30-minute scaffolded learning units with tutorials, feedback and examples; designed with evidence-centred design (citing Mislevy, Steinberg & Almond 2003).
athar_applications: Primary international reference for assessing learning processes in interactive digital environments; ATHAR should align its process-data approach and terminology with it.
limitations: Framework read 2026-10-27 (gap-fill); results and item-level scoring of LDW not yet examined; 15-year-old target population.

title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume III): Creative Minds, Creative Schools
key_findings: First PISA cycle to assess creative thinking (students' capacity to generate original and diverse ideas and to evaluate/improve them); 64 countries/economies took part; published 18 June 2024.
Analyses performance by gender, socio-economic status and school characteristics, and the relation between school opportunities for creative thinking and outcomes.
athar_applications: Shows that an open-ended higher-order construct can be assessed at scale with rubric-scored tasks; useful model for ATHAR's 'generate alternative hypotheses' skill (S4).
limitations: Scoring methods, Arab-country participation and headline results were not retrieved this session; framework itself is in PISA 2022 Assessment and Analytical Framework (doi 10.1787/dfe0bf9c-en).

title: Fostering Students' Creativity and Critical Thinking: What it Means in School
key_findings: OECD worked with school networks in 11 countries to develop and trial pedagogical resources - a portfolio of rubrics and example lesson plans - making creativity and critical thinking visible and teachable in primary and secondary schools.
Project also developed and tested instruments for a validation study of the intervention.
athar_applications: Cross-check ATHAR's critical-thinking rubric language and progression against OECD's rubric portfolio; offers international credibility for school sales.
limitations: Rubric content and study results not retrieved this session; rubrics are designed for teachers, not automated scoring.

title: Media and Information Literate Citizens: Think Critically, Click Wisely! (UNESCO Model MIL Curriculum for Educators and Learners, 2nd ed.)
key_findings: Second edition of UNESCO's Model MIL Curriculum (launched April 2021), described by UNESCO as the only international curriculum harmonising information, media and digital competencies; addresses AI, digital citizenship, disinformation and online hate speech; for formal, non-formal and informal learning.
Author list from OpenAlex record; the earlier 2011 curriculum exists in twelve languages.
athar_applications: Anchor for ATHAR's digital/media-investigation cases (source verification, lateral reading, image provenance) and for school-alignment claims.
limitations: Licence and Arabic availability of the 2nd edition not confirmed this session; check UNESDOC record before reuse.

title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
key_findings: Review of experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring and no tutoring: human tutoring effect d ≈ 0.79 (much lower than the widely believed 2.0); step-based intelligent tutoring systems d ≈ 0.76 - nearly as effective as human tutors.
Commonly held beliefs that finer interaction granularity gives ever-larger gains were not confirmed. Vol. 46(4), pp. 197-221.
athar_applications: Supports evaluating learner steps (each investigative action) rather than only final answers; adaptive step-level feedback is the realistic target, not 'AI tutor = 2 sigma'.
limitations: Mostly STEM procedural domains; effect sizes vs no tutoring, not vs strong alternatives.

title: The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis
key_findings: Small positive effects of gamification on cognitive (g = 0.49, k = 19), motivational (g = 0.36, k = 16) and behavioural (g = 0.25, k = 9) learning outcomes.

Only the cognitive effect was stable in methodologically rigorous studies; motivational and behavioural effects were less stable; heterogeneity substantial. Combining competition with collaboration was particularly effective for behavioural outcomes.
Published online Aug 2019; vol. 32(1), pp. 77-112 (2020).
athar_applications: Points/badges layers are a secondary lever; if used, prefer team-based (collaborative competition) structures; measure, don't assume, motivational gains.
limitations: Few studies per moderator; many short interventions; gamification ≠ game-based learning.

title: Formative assessment: a critical review
publisher: Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice (Routledge)
key_findings: Argues widely quoted quantitative effectiveness claims for formative assessment rest on sources that are untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished, so reported effects warrant scepticism.

'Formative assessment' is not yet a well-defined set of practices; effects should vary widely; calls for domain-grounded, measurement-sound approaches with substantial teacher support. Vol. 18(1), pp. 5-25.
athar_applications: Do not cite large formative-assessment effect sizes in ATHAR marketing; define ATHAR's formative cycle precisely so it can be evaluated.
limitations: Critique, not new empirical data.

title: Three Generations of DIF Analyses: Considering Where It Has Been, Where It Is Now, and Where It Is Going
key_findings: Reviews DIF theory and practice and proposes three generations of DIF analysis, with organising principles for cataloguing and comparing detection methods. Vol. 4(2), pp. 223-233.
athar_applications: Method anchor for ATHAR's dialect-group fairness checks: test whether cases/observables behave differently for equal-ability learners from different dialect regions.
limitations: Methodological review; specific procedures must be chosen by a psychometrician; DIF requires adequate group sample sizes.

title: Length-Controlled AlpacaEval: A Simple Way to Debias Automatic Evaluators
key_findings: LLM auto-annotator (AlpacaEval) favoured models producing longer outputs; a regression (GLM) correction estimating preference at zero length difference made the metric robust to verbosity and raised Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.
athar_applications: Concrete technique for ATHAR scorer audits: model score as a function of answer length and other features, and report length-controlled agreement.
limitations: arXiv comment lists COLM 2024 (peer-reviewed venue); evidence grade C retained pending owner review; evaluates chatbot outputs, not student work.
AUDIT 2026-10-27: licence confirmed as CC BY 4.0 via the arXiv abstract page licence link; rights corrected from UNKNOWN (attribution required).

title: ALDi: Quantifying the Arabic Level of Dialectness of Text
key_findings: Proposes a continuous Arabic Level of Dialectness (ALDi) score instead of binary dialect labels; introduces AOC-ALDi (~128K sentences, human-rated); model generalises to unseen dialects and genres.
athar_applications: Use a dialectness score as a covariate in scorer fairness audits: check whether LLM rubric scores drift with dialectness at equal reasoning quality.
limitations: Preprint version checked (venue not confirmed this session); trained mostly on user comments/news, not teen writing.

title: Having Beer after Prayer? Measuring Cultural Bias in Large Language Models
key_findings: Multilingual and Arabic-only LMs favoured Western-associated entities over Arab-culture ones; CAMeL resource (628 prompts, 20,368 entities) used to evaluate 16 models showed stereotyping and cultural unfairness in Arabic tasks.
Common pretraining sources like Wikipedia may be ill-suited for culturally aware models without adjustment.
athar_applications: LLM-generated feedback or scoring in ATHAR may misjudge Arab-culture references (names, foods, practices) in learner answers; include culturally specific items in scorer audits.
limitations: Preprint version checked (v4, 2024); venue not confirmed this session.

title: Integrating Learning, Problem Solving, and Engagement in Narrative-Centered Learning Environments
publisher: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (IOS Press)
key_findings: Study of 153 middle-school students in a narrative-centred (mystery-style science) learning environment: learning, in-game problem solving and engagement were positively related, not in conflict, even controlling for prior knowledge and game experience.
Males and students with more game experience reported greater presence; presence differences related more to game experience than gender. Vol. 21(1-2), pp. 115-133.
athar_applications: Closest research analogue to ATHAR (narrative mystery + science inquiry); supports logging in-game problem-solving progress as a predictor of learning.
Equity check: novice gamers may feel less presence - include an onboarding case and test engagement by gaming experience and gender.
limitations: Correlational; the environment is not named in the abstract retrieved (widely known as Crystal Island - confirm from full text); single environment, US students.

title: Is Literary Arabic a Second Language for Native Arab Speakers?: Evidence from Semantic Priming Study
key_findings: Auditory lexical decision with semantic priming across Spoken Arabic, Literary Arabic and Hebrew: within-Spoken-Arabic priming was about twice the between-language priming, and Literary Arabic behaved like Hebrew (an L2) in one experiment.
Authors conclude spoken and literary Arabic retain first- and second-language status in the cognitive system. Vol. 34(1), pp. 51-70.
athar_applications: Treat MSA reading/writing load as potential construct-irrelevant variance for reasoning scores; allow dialect or voice responses and simplify case text.
limitations: Adult sample from one dialect community; lab lexical task - generalisation to teen reading comprehension is an inference.

title: Kolb's experiential learning model: critique from a modelling perspective
key_findings: Applying modelling and categorisation criteria, identifies problems in Kolb's experiential learning model: graphic syntax errors, failures of sufficiency and simplification tests, categorisation/definition problems, misconstrued bipolarities and flawed logic; proposes guidelines to recast it. Vol. 32(1), pp. 29-46.
athar_applications: Use 'experience -> reflection -> generalisation -> new application' only as a loose design heuristic for the debrief, not as a validated theory or for learner typing.
limitations: Conceptual critique; does not test learning outcomes.

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
publisher: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers)
key_findings: LLM evaluators (e.g., GPT-4 as referee) show positional bias: swapping the order of candidate responses can flip quality rankings - with ChatGPT as evaluator, Vicuna-13B appeared to beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries.
Proposes a calibration framework (with human annotation used for evaluation) that reduces bias and aligns better with human judgements. Pages 9440-9450.
athar_applications: Never let an LLM compare two learners' answers side by side; score each answer independently against the rubric, and test order effects in audits.
limitations: Chatbot-response evaluation, not student reasoning; calibration specifics not retrieved this session.

title: A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation
key_findings: 128 studies: engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d ≈ -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); positive (informational) feedback enhanced free-choice behaviour (d ≈ 0.33) and interest (d ≈ 0.31).
Tangible rewards tended to be more detrimental for children than college students; verbal rewards less enhancing for children.
athar_applications: Avoid tangible/completion rewards for simply finishing cases (e.g., coins per case); prefer informational feedback about reasoning; reward the quality of inference, not completion.
limitations: Lab tasks with interesting activities; the undermining effect is debated in parts of the literature (counter-reviews not verified this session).

title: Defining, Conceptualizing, and Measuring Fidelity of Implementation and Its Relationship to Outcomes in K-12 Curriculum Intervention Research
key_findings: Review finds too few K-12 curriculum intervention studies measure fidelity of implementation and relate it to outcomes; argues fidelity measurement is needed for internal and external validity and differs between efficacy and effectiveness studies. Vol. 78(1), pp. 33-84.
athar_applications: ATHAR's school studies must log implementation (minutes played, debriefs held, teacher mode used) and analyse outcomes by fidelity.
limitations: Curriculum interventions, not apps; conceptual guidance.

title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26), e2422633122
key_findings: Field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school math students (Turkey) comparing a plain GPT-4 interface ('GPT Base') and a tutor with learning safeguards ('GPT Tutor').
With access during practice, grades rose 48% (Base) and 127% (Tutor); when access was removed, the Base group scored 17% lower than students who never had access.
Safeguards in GPT Tutor largely mitigated the negative learning effect; students used unrestricted GPT-4 as a crutch. An erratum was published (Aug 2025).
athar_applications: Design rule: ATHAR's AI characters and hint agent must never hand over conclusions; they ask, point to evidence, and require the learner's own justification.
Measure learning on unassisted post-tests, not on assisted in-game performance.
limitations: Mathematics, one country, short term; abstract-level reading; erratum content not reviewed.

title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
key_findings: RCT with college physics students: a custom AI tutor built on the same pedagogical principles as the active-learning class produced significantly more learning in less time.
Students also reported more engagement and motivation with the AI tutor.
athar_applications: Positive evidence is for a pedagogically designed tutor, not a generic chatbot: consistent with ATHAR's constrained, principle-driven AI guide.
limitations: University sample at one institution; short units; abstract-level reading; not adolescents. Open access via PMC; licence not confirmed on the article page.

title: Evaluating Rater Effects of Large Language Models in Automated Essay Scoring: GPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek
key_findings: Compared 10 LLMs (incl. GPT-4o, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5/2.0, DeepSeek V3/R1) with expert raters on two writing tasks using accuracy, intra-rater consistency and many-facet Rasch rater effects.
GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed higher accuracy, better consistency and fewer rater effects; authors caution the small sample does not support a ranking.
athar_applications: Use rater-effect models (severity/leniency, consistency) in ATHAR's LLM-scorer acceptance protocol, not only correlation with humans; re-run when the model version changes.
limitations: English writing tasks; small sample; models age quickly; abstract-level reading.

title: ChatGPT as an automated essay scoring tool in the writing classrooms: how it compares with human scoring
key_findings: 200 argumentative EFL essays (four proficiency levels) scored by ChatGPT and an experienced human rater.
ChatGPT scores showed only weak-to-moderate relationships with the human rater and low intraclass consistency across two scoring rounds; authors attribute this to the model, updates and randomness.
athar_applications: Counter-evidence to optimistic LLM-scoring results: ATHAR must test repeat-scoring stability (same response, multiple runs) and fix model versions before any summative use.
limitations: One human rater; ChatGPT version and prompting specifics not visible at abstract level; EFL English essays.
